text_fidelity_a:
Philips SHE9850 in-Ear Headphones with Advanced Acoustics (Discontinued by Manufacturer) Some people prefer their headphones outside of their ears, with comfortable ear cushions and other features, such as the [[ASIN:B00007056H Koss KTXPRO1 Titanium Portable Headphones with Volume Control]]. Others prefer wearing their headphones in the privacy of their own ears, with the added bonus of noise isolation.

There are good reasons for choosing either type depending on your personal preferences, such as comfort levels, where and when you're using them, what you're listening to, and whether or not you have to share with other people.

For general use at home, I use the regular "outie", especially for movies or music with inappropriate language that I'd rather not play in surround sound in the presence of young `uns. I also let my son use it when I'd rather not hear another note from the Jonas Brothers. However, in the wee hours of the morning when the only creature stirring is me, I prefer to use in-ear headphones, which shut out everything except the music.

At work, I hardly ever use headphones due to the telephone ringing off the hook, but at lunchtime I sometimes use the in-ear headphones for peace and quiet. I drive to work, so no headphones are needed for the daily commute.

This is a fairly expensive model, but it's worth every cent if you can safely use headphones that cut out most external noise.

Pros:

1. Really nice packaging, easy to open, simple instruction manual
2. Cool, sleek and compact black metal carrying case included, with a cleaning tool and cable clip as accessories.
3. It comes with three different sizes of rubber caps, and as Goldilocks might say, one is for ears that are big, one's for smaller ears, and one will no doubt be just right. Changing caps is simple too.
4. It also includes a pair of memory foam sleeves that fit so snugly in your ears that you may think they belong there.
5. The caps are washable, once you dry them properly before using them again.
6. The sound is marvelous, clear and true, and there's no need to raise the volume to sonic boom levels.
7. The headphones are clearly marked left and right, and are at an angle for easy insertion and a tight seal
8. Drastically cuts down on external noise

Cons:

1. Unless you're using it for an IPod or other portable device, the cord is too short.
2. May feel a bit weird for some people due to the superior noise isolation.
3. You may experience "ewwwwwwwwwww" moments when your friends grab them and try them on. These aren't for sharing.
4. Try saying "in-ear headphones" out loud six times

If you're looking for an excellent pair of (deep breath) in-ear headphones, I think you'll be pleased with this one.

Amanda Richards, July 2, 2008
text_fidelity_b: Philips SHE9850 in-Ear Headphones with Advanced Acoustics (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

It's metal, not plastic, and has a nice heft and feels durable. It looks great. And audio quality is very good. It comes with a micro SD card already installed and ready to go. It also comes with a set of ear buds, a lavalier microphone which can be used instead of the built-in mics, a cord for line-in recording, and a USB charging cord. No charger is included. And it does not come with a protective pouch or sleeve. But it is boxed nicely.

It records in user-selectable WAV or MP3 formats in various selectable bitrates. It has adjustable gain control and a noise reduction function. One important function for voice recording is the ability to monitor while recording using ear buds or headphones, and this recorder has that capability. The display screen isn't as sharp and clear as it is portrayed in the listing photos, but it is decent.

Now for the minor negatives, for which I dinged a star off the review rating. One is the printing labeling the buttons on the one I received is only a little lighter than the color of the recorder, making them very hard to read. That means you have to memorize the button location and functions or keep the user manual handy for reference. And that leads to the second negative, and that is the print in the user manual is tiny. Really tiny. I looked for a PDF version online and couldn't find one. The manual suggests visiting the brand's web site, but neither the manual nor the box provide a URL. Or even the listing brand name (Tenmatec) for that matter. I wound taking photographs of the manual pages with a tablet so I could enlarge them for easier reading. The other minor negative is that it has no USB-C port, only a micro USB for recharging or connecting to a computer for moving files around.

Other than that it's a good recorder. It has one-button functionality (although there is a slight delay when starting a recording while it starts up). Because of its metal construction and heft it feels good in-hand and looks really good.
text_fidelity_b: TenmaTec Voice Recorder with Playback,80GB Voice Activated Recorder with DSP Noise Reduction,Dual Microphones, Mp3,Speaker,Password Protect,for Music,Overdubbing,Studio,Dictation,Interview

For the extra money, you get 4 condensers (instead of 3) to give you higher-resolution 24-bit audio (instead of 16-bit) plus a bunch of fancier control and display options. The new microphone has the same directional recording patterns to isolate the recording to your intended audio sources. Is the new microphone worth the extra money? If you really need 24-bit audio, then definitely yes. If not, the new display and control features are more convenient than a huge jump in functionality. The Blue Yeti is still a great microphone for amateur USB recording (podcasts, musical performances, etc). The new version is a step forward, but not worth the price for everyone.

My biggest complaint is that the new microphone uses the same ancient mini-USB interface as the old one. Modern ultralight laptops are moving to the USB-C standard and mini-USB is 2 generations old. You could use a USB-C hub to give you a mini-USB interface, but I wish all modern devices came with USB-C ports since this has been the standard for the last few years.

I haven’t explored ALL features but i was pretty excited about the “Drop in” feature... BUT it wasn’t that great. The sound is horrible. For other uses, I’m loving it so far! Bummer about the drop in feature. I was hoping to use this feature often to call home to talk to my son when I’m at work to check on him...

text_fidelity_a:
Portable Pocket WOWOTO Projector Android Mini Smart LED DLP Projector I was actually really shocked at how great this little portable speaker is. My cell phone found it in seconds, and in less than a minute I was listening to music from my cell phone, only out of this little speaker, it actually sounded great. In fact, the bass was so effective out of this thing that some of my favorite songs made it dance around the table.

I love that it is so much louder than the music I get out of my cell phone, and I also love that I can listen to hip-hop and rap and enjoy actual bass, which usually doesn't come through for my cell phone speaker at all.

You can actually control the music from your cell phone from the speaker itself. It has a pause/play button, forward and back, and volume controls. It also has a speakerphone control, in case you wanted to have a quick conversation from the speaker itself. I would not personally want to use the speaker as a speakerphone, but it is nice to have the option in a pinch.

The one thing I didn't care for is that when you tap the volume button and it hits its maximum, it beeps at you to let you know that it won't go any louder. It's a pretty annoying sound, and in my view they could just have left that feature out. I'm sure I would figure it out soon enough that it wouldn't go any louder.

Overall, I was really surprised at the quality, ease of setup, and range of sound from this cute little speaker. I'm delighted to own it, and anticipate it getting a lot of use over the coming months and years.
text_fidelity_b: Portable Pocket WOWOTO Projector Android Mini Smart LED DLP Projector

text_fidelity_a:
Patriot LX Series 64GB High Speed Micro SDXC Class 10 UHS-I Transfer Speeds For Action Cameras, Phones, Tablets, and PCs So I bought this to use with my 128GB Lenovo Yoga as a secondary drive. When I plugged it into my computer to transfer some files, it shows 116GBs - what it should be for a 128GB drive. Though I really wish computers and manufacturers would calculate memory the same, that is another matter.

I went to transfer a folder with 61 GBs of memory. It got about 3/4 done and it decided it was full. With about 50GBs, my 116 GB card is FULL. It should be only about half full. This is a problem. I am not happy about this and will not buy another one of these. I will format it and try again. Maybe there are hidden files that aren't showing up on it. But this is really annoying.

Update: I decided to format the drive and found that the bit size for exFAT is very small. As in less than my file size small. I changed it to NTSF, as it will only be used in a computer, and it is now working properly as regards to being able to actually fill it with 116 GBs. But it still took about 4 hours to copy 8 GBs of data to it. My USB 3.0 drive would have done it in less than 30 minutes.
text_fidelity_b: Patriot LX Series 64GB High Speed Micro SDXC Class 10 UHS-I Transfer Speeds For Action Cameras, Phones, Tablets, and PCs

Telescopes for Adults Astronomy - 700x90mm AZ Astronomical Professional Refractor Telescope for Kids Beginners Astronomy with Advanced Eyepieces, Cool Christmas Astronomy Gift for Men, White I use the 'refractor' telescope as a long-range spotting scope. The 90mm aperture is the step up from a 50 or 70mm spotting scope.

The larger the aperture (objective lens), the more light enters. The amount of light captured by the 90mm aperture is a 'reflector' mirror comparable to a 114mm 'reflector' telescope, which is the other 'next step up' option for stargazing. However, 'reflectors' are higher maintenance (mirror cleaning and stability), sensitive to temperature, and more sophisticated to operate and collimate. An avid astronomy hobbyist must ultimately step up to the greater magnification, higher-quality optical path, and more expensive 'reflector.' For spotting wildlife & birdwatching, the 90mm refractor is ideal.

The 700mm focal length is comparatively short. To calculate the magnification, divide the focal length by the aperture. 700mm/90mm = 7.8 better known as f/7.8. For comparison, a 1000mm focal length, typical with a 90mm aperture, is a significantly more powerful f/11.1. But, tube length is important for remaining concealed in spotting scope mode, which is my specific interest. The 700mm length works well in a confined stand.

This refractor type is simple to operate. Assemble it, and you're in business. Plus, the magnified image is right-side up. This telescope is about as easy to set up as I've seen.

The scope comes with an above-average stand. Unfortunately, the horizontal plane locking screw mechanism is insufficient to secure the tube weight in horizontal spotting mode. The fix is easy. The telescope tube employs the fix in its lens eyepiece adapter.

Foreign objects are visible in the main eyepiece. However, the eyepiece internal optical path appears to be inaccessible.

By comparison, this 700x90 scope seems overpriced for the quality.

One month later: I replaced the artifact encumbered 25mm eyepiece with a 32mm Plössl eyepiece. Huge improvement in eye relief, full broadband multilayer coatings, and a whopping 50° increase in FOV.
text_fidelity_b: Telescopes for Adults Astronomy - 700x90mm AZ Astronomical Professional Refractor Telescope for Kids Beginners Astronomy with Advanced Eyepieces, Cool Christmas Astronomy Gift for Men, White
